title: Why AI chatbots make things up
summary: An LLM writes by picking a likely next word, over and over. It never looks anything up, so when it does not know, it still picks the likeliest sounding word. Putting the real answer in the prompt changes which word is likeliest, which is why RAG works.
html:
Lesson 1 said the AI sometimes gives a confident answer that is not true. Today is why. Once you see it, the reason RAG works becomes obvious.

It is autocomplete, scaled up enormously

Your phone keyboard suggests the next word as you type. Type "see you" and it offers "tomorrow". It is not thinking about your plans. It has just seen "see you tomorrow" many times, so "tomorrow" is a likely next word.

An LLM works the same way, with far more practice. Before anyone uses it, it reads a huge amount of text and learns which words tend to follow which. That reading phase is called training. After training, it writes an answer one word at a time: look at everything so far, pick a likely next word, add it, repeat. That is called next word prediction, and it is genuinely all the model is doing.

A small example with numbers

Ask it to finish: "The capital of France is ___". Inside, it scores possible next words, roughly like this:

Paris    95%
Lyon      2%
a         1%
...

It picks Paris. Correct, because it saw that fact thousands of times during training.

Now ask: "At our company, employees get ___ days of leave". It never saw your company's handbook. But it has seen plenty of text about leave in general, so the scores look something like:

20    30%
25    20%
15    15%
30    10%
...

Here is the important part. There is no step where it checks whether it actually knows. It just picks a likely word, "20", and keeps writing in the same smooth, confident style it always uses. The sentence sounds exactly as sure as the one about Paris. That is a hallucination: not a lie, just the likeliest sounding guess, delivered fluently.

An analogy: a quiz contestant who is never allowed to say "pass". Asked something they know, they answer well. Asked something they do not know, they still have to say something, so they give the answer that sounds most plausible, in the same confident voice.

Why pasting the answer in fixes it

Now do what lesson 1 did. Put the handbook sentence in the prompt first: "Full time employees receive 24 days of paid leave per year." Then ask the same question. The scores change:

24    97%
20     1%
...

Why? Because the model predicts the next word based on everything in front of it, and "24" is sitting right there in the text it was just given. The most likely next word is now the true one.

That is the whole trick behind RAG. It does not make the model smarter. It changes what the likeliest next word is, by putting the real answer where the model can see it. Giving the AI real source text to base its answer on has a name: grounding.

One honest catch

If you paste in the wrong paragraph, or nothing useful, the model goes back to guessing. So grounding only works if you found the right piece of text. Finding it is the next lesson.

New words today

Training: the learning phase, when the model reads a huge amount of text before anyone uses it.

Next word prediction: how an LLM writes, one likely word at a time.

Grounding: giving the AI real source text to base its answer on.

All of them are in the glossary.

If you remember one thing
The AI always picks a likely next word, whether it knows the answer or not. RAG works by putting the real answer in front of it, so the likely word becomes the true one.

Next lesson: how you find the right paragraph in the first place, starting with plain old keyword search.
exercise:
Catch it guessing, five minutes. Ask ChatGPT: "Summarise the book The Quiet Index by Meera Rao." That book does not exist. Watch whether it admits that or confidently invents a plot. Then ask it "Is that book real?" and see what it says. You have just watched next word prediction produce a hallucination.

Then reply to the email. One line: "done", or the first word that confused you.
